title: Composite Indexes
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of composite indexes.
Apply indexing multiple columns in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn composite indexes through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Composite Indexes matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: For composite indexes, begin with evidence from representative queries and data. Read the execution plan and compare measured behavior before changing indexes or query structure; keep both correctness and write costs in view.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Indexing multiple columns, Column order, Leftmost-prefix considerations where applicable, Filtering and sorting combinations. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Indexing multiple columns
items.text: Indexing multiple columns should be evaluated with measurements on representative data. Inspect the plan, estimated versus actual row counts where available, and the workload's read/write balance; an index or rewrite is not automatically faster.

items.title: Column order
items.text: Column order helps you understand query access paths and use indexes selectively, weighing measured read improvements against storage and write costs. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Leftmost-prefix considerations where applicable
items.text: Leftmost-prefix considerations where applicable begins with a definition of the metric and its grain. Name the numerator, denominator, time zone, null policy, and tie-handling rule before translating the definition into SQL.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

hints: Begin with the subtopic indexing multiple columns and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
